summary: Stone-and-brick light on Presque Isle Harbor, Lake Huron, lit 1840 and replaced in 1871; now a township museum with a climbable tower in season.

lens.where: Acquired by the Stebbins family at a Coast Guard auction; the sources do not say where it is now.

structures.note: Tapered brick-and-stone tower; 12 ft across at the base, 6 ft at the lantern (LighthouseFriends). Height disputed: 31 ft (LighthouseFriends); 100 ft from base to lantern (archive).
One-and-a-half-story brick dwelling, 35 by 20 ft (LighthouseFriends). Roof collapsed by 1930; demolished 1939; a residence built on its foundation in 1939.

access.note: Township museum. Open in season (late May to mid-October); tower climbs in season (2025 fee $6 adults, $4 children). Closed for the winter after the 2026 season.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends gives the tower as thirty-one feet (about 9.4 m). The archive gives 100 feet from base to lantern (about 30.5 m). The record's 11.0 m (36 ft) matches neither. A person should check before changing it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1840 as the year the original lens was installed. LighthouseFriends describes the 1840 light as eleven lamps in reflectors, with a fourth-order Fresnel lens installed in 1857. The story follows LighthouseFriends for the 1857 Fresnel and treats 1840 as the start of the light's lamps.

notes_for_editor: NRHP 73000957: the NPS PDF is not digitised (placeholder); the National Register date (11 April 1973), the Michigan Register date (14 November 1964) and the 1965 marker are from LighthouseFriends only. Heights disagree: LighthouseFriends 31 ft; archive 100 ft base-to-lantern and 123 ft above water; record 11.0 m. The story gives LighthouseFriends' figure and states the archive's. Unresolved. The archive's 'Other Structures' line (1.5-story brick keepers quarters 'attached to 1870 tower', 1905 keepers, garage, privy) does not fit the 1840 dwelling, which LighthouseFriends says was demolished in 1939. The 1870 tower is probably the new light; not used. Lemuel Crawford is named only by LighthouseFriends (interim keeper, 27 August to September 1840); he is not on the archive roster; his row is 'acting keeper'. Patrick Garrity moved to the new light (us-mi-new-presque-isle), which is not researched here. The 1837 Pendergrast report, the 1838 Homans report and the 1868 Board statement are quoted as LighthouseFriends quotes them; the originals were not read. The Lighthouse Board corpus starts in 1891, so the 1840s-1870s reports are not in it. The Parris caretakers and LighthouseFriends' ghost-light anecdote are left out: they are private people and the anecdote has no source beyond LighthouseFriends. Storms, wrecks and rescues: no record for this light in the sources read; that chapter is not written. One newspaper search (Chronicling America, Michigan, 1870-1871) returned nothing usable; no newspaper pages were read. Visit information read 2026-10-27: closed for the winter after the 2026 season; the 2025 climb fee is stated; the 2026 fee was not stated. Check hours before publishing. Photos: none sourced. Fact-check 2026-10-27 (independent pass): quote check found all 55 quotes on the first run. Checked the sentences against LighthouseFriends, the USLHS record (tower and lens 1840, original lens removed, five principal keepers, 100 feet to the lantern and 123 feet above the water), the township visit and hours pages (fees, 42-inch rule, winter closing after the 2026 season). Changed: metres added to every feet value in the building and tower sentences (the 100 and 123 foot figures are in the story as 30.5 m and 37.5 m); 'run the tours' changed to 'run it', since LighthouseFriends says the Parris couple was hired 'to run the place' in 1977. The LighthouseFriends intro supplies the French gloss for Presque Isle and the 'few Great Lakes peninsulas' line, so no footnote changes were needed there. Nothing else was altered. Still open for a human: the tower height (31 feet, LighthouseFriends, against 100 feet from base to lantern in the archive, which the story states), and the 1840 date for the first light (the archive's lens date; the keeper appointments in LighthouseFriends imply the light was lit by 27 August 1840).
